6 Top NFT Trends to Watch Out For (2024 & 2025)
===============================================

![Image 72: Oliver Smith](https://nftevening.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/img-author-oliver-smith.png)
By [Oliver Smith](https://nftevening.com/authors/oliver-smith/)

February 3, 2025

[![Image 74: google-news](https://nftevening.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/google-news-icon.png)](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqKQgKIiNDQklTRkFnTWFoQUtEbTVtZEdWMlpXNXBibWN1WTI5dEtBQVAB?ceid=US:en&oc=3&hl=en-US&gl=US)

Key Takeaways

*   According to [CryptoSlam](https://www.cryptoslam.io/), the total NFT sales volume is over US$65 billion, with Ethereum, Solana, and Bitcoin being the top blockchains for NFT traders.

*   The top NFT trends to watch out for are the rise of utility NFTs, the tokenization of real-world assets, NFTs in the music industry, hybrid NFTs, Bitcoin NFTs, and the gaming expansion of digital collectibles.

*   The Global Non-fungible Token (NFT) Market is expected to reach US$152.54 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 34.2% from 2024 to 2030 (_Source:_[_VMR report_](https://virtuemarketresearch.com/report/non-fungible-token-nft-market)).

![Image 76: 6 Top NFT Trends to Watch Out For (2024 & 2025)](https://nftevening.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/What-is-the-next-nff-trend.jpg)

The world of [Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs)](https://nftevening.com/what-is-an-nft/) is changing quickly. As technology and creativity come together, new NFT trends are appearing. These trends are set to shape the future of digital arts in 2024 and 2025. This guide explores these top upcoming NFT trends, giving you insights into the future of NFT use cases.

**The Top NFT Trends in 2024**
------------------------------

### **1. Utility NFTs**

In the early days, NFTs were primarily used for digital art and collectibles. However, the trend is shifting towards other emerging NFT sectors such as utility NFTs. These tokens are not just about owning a digital asset; they offer additional functionalities and benefits. For instance, utility NFTs can provide access to exclusive content, events, or communities. They can also represent ownership of real-world assets such as real estate or vehicles.

The demand for utility NFTs is growing as they offer more value to the holder. In 2024 and 2025, we can expect to see more projects integrating utility features into their NFTs. This trend will likely attract a broader audience, including those interested in the practical applications of NFTs beyond art and collectibles.

_For example, the_[_Bored Ape Yacht Club ($BAYC)_](https://nftevening.com/bored-ape-yacht-club-the-avatar-collectibles-with-the-biggest-community/)_has introduced practical benefits through their NFTs. For example, they organize_[_ApeFest_](https://apefest.com/)_, an annual event exclusively for NFT holders. Participants can gather to showcase their collections and enjoy activities such as live music, auctions, and games. This adds extra value to owning a $BAYC NFT, making it more than just a digital asset._

![Image 78: Utility NFTs](https://lh7-us.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXf9QBEDAQO1Crsrlt8pa8XTnqpVbrameIlebpM3-PmGexDlWOQtZ2Eys4GiJvFbIjtSO4lFrvCOaZaIFFuIcE7z7qhL4fnyi0VyCWg3JJOu7yycZg5hkvRf7cIktClIf-vJzGoQGY6eymxUQVIac576T9dX?key=ylw-9rTUa6FrVBEU24_-0w)
Events for the BAYC/MAYC holders. Source: Apefest

### **2. Real-World Assets (RWA) NFTs**

The tokenization of real-world assets is a trend that is gaining traction. NFTs can represent ownership of physical items like real estate, art, and even luxury goods. This tokenization provides a way to divide ownership, making it easier for people to invest in high-value assets. You can also call it fractional NFTs.

For example, an NFT can represent a share in a piece of real estate, allowing multiple investors to own a part of the property. This approach makes investments that were previously out of reach for many people more accessible. In 2024 and 2025, we can expect to see more real-world assets being tokenized, opening up new investment opportunities.

_According to a_[_report_](https://www.binance.com/en-IN/blog/research/binance-research-examining-the-state-of-realworld-assets-4697414668665991002)_, the real-world asset tokenization or the tokenization of global illiquid assets to be a $16T business opportunity by 2030._

### **3. Hybrid NFTs**

Hybrid NFTs blend digital assets with real-world items. For example, owning a digital artwork NFT might also give you a physical print. This mix makes the NFTs more appealing and valuable. It bridges the gap between the digital and physical worlds.

_One notable example is Nike’s Cryptokicks. These are digital shoes that come with a physical pair. Cryptokicks generated over $10 million in sales in their first month. This shows the strong demand for hybrid NFTs._

![Image 80: Hybrid NFTs](https://lh7-us.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXc7v5juo3d35cFuQU5NhAh_q2ooNeWGoOVfxYL0kbBydvDKQVgm4pSm6ul3-n8B_SkN5d_ykw1p354cj7LeH-1cn97IkKANDqjgSHhyVjFOdIqidSi25Um0cvDz_go2S42lhEV7_zVDNqSb1F1sP2o-K52T?key=ylw-9rTUa6FrVBEU24_-0w)
RTFKT x Nike Dunk Genesis CRYPTOKICKS: Source: OpenSea

Hybrid NFT trends are likely to grow in the coming years. As more brands and creators explore this trend, we can expect more innovative products. Hybrid NFTs could become a standard in various industries, from fashion to entertainment.

### **4. NFTs in the Music Industry**

The music industry is another area where NFTs are making a significant impact. Artists can tokenize their music, offering exclusive tracks, albums, or concert tickets as NFTs. This approach provides a new revenue stream for artists and a unique way for fans to support their favorite musicians.

NFTs in the music industry can also include royalties. For instance, an NFT can be programmed to pay a percentage of future sales back to the original artist, ensuring ongoing revenue. As more musicians and record labels explore the potential of NFTs, this trend will continue to grow, transforming how music is distributed and monetized.

_According to_[_some estimates_](https://soundcamps.com/spotify-royalties-calculator/)_, an artist only gets about 4 cents for every song played on Spotify. That means to make just $4,000, an artist would need a whopping one million streams. Therefore,_[_Music NFTs_](https://nftevening.com/nft-music/)_can be a more lucrative and alternative option._

### **5. Gaming NFT Expansion**

The gaming industry has always been a place for innovation, and NFTs are no exception. In 2024 and 2025, expect NFT gaming to explode into a full-fledged phenomenon.

Here’s why: NFT-based games allow players to truly own in-game items, like weapons, skins, or virtual land. This ownership opens doors for a whole new level of engagement – players can trade, sell, or even rent out their in-game assets, creating a thriving digital economy within the game itself.

As more game developers adopt this model, we can expect a big increase in NFT-based games and a growing market for in-game NFTs. For example, Axie Infinity has already generated over $4 billion in sales volume, showing the potential of NFTs in gaming.

Date:2005 - present

Headquarters:[Seoul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Seoul)

Areas Of Involvement:[music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music)[sound recording](https://www.britannica.com/technology/sound-recording)[K-pop](https://www.britannica.com/art/K-pop)

HYBE Corp. is a South Korean global entertainment company established in 2005 by Bang Si-hyuk, an entrepreneur, composer, and [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) executive. Founded as Big Hit Entertainment Co., Ltd., the company has grown to become a [multinational corporation](https://www.britannica.com/money/multinational-corporation) with subsidiaries specializing in music production and publishing, talent and event management, and concert production.

Upon its founding, HYBE entered the [K-pop industry](https://www.britannica.com/art/K-pop)—a genre of popular music originating in [South Korea](https://www.britannica.com/place/South-Korea) that blends elements of [pop](https://www.britannica.com/art/popular-music), [hip-hop](https://www.britannica.com/art/hip-hop), [rhythm and blues](https://www.britannica.com/art/rhythm-and-blues), and [electronic music](https://www.britannica.com/art/electronic-music). It competed directly with the big three K-pop producers at the time: SM Entertainment, YG Entertainment, and JYP Entertainment.

HYBE disrupted common management and production practices in the K-pop industry by engaging fans directly through [social media](https://www.britannica.com/topic/social-media) and diversifying its content beyond music to include webtoons, [games](https://www.britannica.com/technology/online-gaming), and original stories. This differentiated strategy—most evident through its flagship act, [BTS](https://www.britannica.com/topic/BTS)—helped transform the company into a global entertainment [conglomerate](https://www.britannica.com/money/conglomerate-business).

HYBE has been a leader in popularizing K-pop in the U.S. and other Western countries. The company’s embrace of social media and fan-driven content has changed how music is made and shared, helping to bring fans and artists together worldwide.

HYBE’s global operations and business structure
-----------------------------------------------

HYBE Corp. operates from HYBE HQ, its headquarters in [Seoul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Seoul) that houses its core creative and administrative teams, and owns three international subsidiaries:

*   **HYBE America.** The U.S. division, headquartered in [Santa Monica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Santa-Monica), [California](https://www.britannica.com/place/California-state), oversees operations in the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States). 
*   **HYBE Music Group APAC.** Based in Seoul, this division oversees all music-related functions in South Korea and Japan, including HYBE Japan, based in [Tokyo](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tokyo). 
*   **HYBE Latin America.** The division focuses on expanding HYBE’s presence in Latin American markets, with offices in [Mexico City](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mexico-City), [Miami](https://www.britannica.com/place/Miami-Florida), and [Los Angeles](https://www.britannica.com/place/Los-Angeles-California).

HYBE’s operations have three pillars:

*   **Labels** includes HYBE’s music and entertainment production division. 
*   **Solutions** supports the company’s labels division by managing performances, [intellectual property](https://www.britannica.com/topic/intellectual-property-law), multimedia content, educational initiatives, and games. 
*   **Platforms** includes technology and [social media](https://www.britannica.com/topic/social-media) sites and apps, namely Weverse, an [e-commerce](https://www.britannica.com/money/e-commerce) website and app that connects fans with artists and sells official merchandise.

HYBE’s top artists and collaborations
-------------------------------------

In South Korea, HYBE’s top acts include the company’s lead group BTS, Seventeen, Tomorrow X Together (TXT), Lee Hyun, and the boy band &Team. Among its popular female groups are NewJeans and Le Sserafim.

HYBE America’s top artists have included [Ariana Grande](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ariana-Grande), [Justin Bieber](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Justin-Bieber), and Lil Baby through their association with Scooter Braun’s talent management. Braun became CEO of HYBE America in January 2023. Katseye, one of HYBE America’s earliest signings in collaboration with Geffen Records, marks a significant step in the company’s vision toward creating content that represents an array of cultures.

Big Hit Entertainment: The early years (2005–2012)
--------------------------------------------------

Big Hit Entertainment (Big Hit), the company that evolved into the [global music](https://www.britannica.com/art/global-music) powerhouse known as HYBE Corp., was founded on February 1, 2005, by Bang Si-hyuk, a composer, producer, and hitmaker from record label and production company JYP Entertainment.

The first K-pop act the company signed to gain traction on the South [Korean music](https://www.britannica.com/art/Korean-music) charts was vocal trio 8Eight, which debuted in 2007. The group included singer Lee Hyun, whose solo career continued after 8Eight disbanded seven years later.

In 2010, Big Hit partnered with JYP Entertainment, Bang’s former employer, to comanage 2AM, its second South Korean boy group that would also see widespread success in the K-pop market.

That same year, Bang signed an independent South Korean rapper—Kim Nam-joon, aka Runch Randa (Rap Monster) but better known now as RM—who was part of the underground hip-hop scene. He went on to become the first member of BTS. In its early years, Big Hit faced several challenges, including a scandal in 2012 involving the girl group Glam. Group member Kim Da-hee was sentenced to one year in prison for blackmailing actor Lee Byung-hun. The fallout from the incident led to Glam’s disbandment three years later.

BTS and HYBE’s breakthrough years (2013–2017)
---------------------------------------------

In 2013, Big Hit debuted [BTS](https://www.britannica.com/topic/BTS), its top-billed act and the driving force behind its global success. The group embodied Big Hit’s vision of a new kind of K-pop: Alongside rigorous training and multilingual education, Bang Si-hyuk adopted a less restrictive management style for his artists, especially in songwriting and fan interaction.

By adopting these practices, Big Hit overtook its big three competitors in market capitalization, sales, and global impact, writing the blueprint for modern K-pop success.

In 2014, Big Hit severed its partnership with JYP, losing artists 2AM and 8Eight. The split proved pivotal, allowing Big Hit to focus most of its resources on developing BTS, then still in its early stages of growth.

In 2017, Big Hit made its first foray aimed at international expansion by founding Big Hit Entertainment Japan, through which the company promoted BTS’ The Wings Tour in Japan and the Japanese versions of “Mic Drop,” which reached No. 1 on Billboard Japan’s Top 100, and singles “DNA,” and “Crystal Snow,” both of which made it to Billboard Japan’s Top 20.

Global expansion and acquisitions (2018–2020)
---------------------------------------------

In 2019, BTS released its all-English single, “Dynamite,” which led to the group’s meteoric success in the U.S. and other Western nations. BTS’ triumph in generating international demand allowed Big Hit to expand and eventually diversify its portfolio of assets.

Also in 2019, Big Hit debuted TXT (Tomorrow X Together), its second boy group, further solidifying its position as a leading K-pop agency both domestically and internationally. That same year, it acquired Superb, a game developer specializing in music-based games, and Source Music, a South Korean record label and talent agency. The following year, Big Hit expanded further by acquiring another music label and talent agency, Pledis Entertainment, home to the group Seventeen.

In April 2019, Big Hit established its U.S. headquarters in Santa Monica, California, forming Big Hit America, with [chief executive officer](https://www.britannica.com/money/chief-executive-officer) Yoon Suk-joon and American record executive [Scott Samuel “Scooter” Braun](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scott-Braun) leading the new subsidiary.

In addition to expanding its influence in the K-pop market, Big Hit’s acquisition highlighted the company’s strategic decision to focus on technologies geared toward interactive fan engagement. This vision was exemplified with the 2019 release of Weverse, an innovative app designed to connect artists with their fans.

In March 2020, _Fast Company_ named Big Hit one of its most innovative companies of the year. Seven months later, the company issued its [IPO](https://www.britannica.com/money/ipo-initial-public-offering) on South Korea’s KOSPI, the country’s main [stock exchange](https://www.britannica.com/money/stock-exchange-finance), achieving a [market capitalization](https://www.britannica.com/money/understanding-market-capitalization) of 8.7 trillion South Korean won ($7.6 billion) by the close of its first trading day.

HYBE’s transformation and restructuring (2021)
----------------------------------------------

In 2021, Big Hit renamed itself HYBE Corp. to better reflect its expansion beyond music and toward a wider range of services. HYBE positioned itself as a global entertainment and media company focused on music, fan engagement, and multimedia content. The name change coincided with a reorganization of the company’s operations into three segments: labels, solutions, and platforms.

Shortly after restructuring, HYBE acquired Ithaca Holdings, a Los Angeles–based media [holding company](https://www.britannica.com/money/holding-company) whose roster included [Justin Bieber](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Justin-Bieber) and [Ariana Grande](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ariana-Grande). The acquisition marked HYBE’s entry into the U.S. market.

Strategic partnerships and innovation (2022–2024)
-------------------------------------------------

In 2022, HYBE inked a deal with [Walt Disney Company](https://www.britannica.com/money/Disney-Company) Asia Pacific to stream original programming on Disney+. The lineup included a BTS concert film from [Los Angeles](https://www.britannica.com/place/Los-Angeles-California), a travel [reality show](https://www.britannica.com/topic/reality-TV) featuring K-pop stars and media celebrities, and a BTS documentary.

HYBE also ventured into [blockchain technology](https://www.britannica.com/money/what-is-blockchain) by launching a [non-fungible token](https://www.britannica.com/topic/non-fungible-token-data) (NFT) project with financial technology (fintech) company Dunamu. The project faced significant challenges, mainly environmental concerns raised by fans and the general public.

In 2023, HYBE kicked off its expansion into [Latin American music](https://www.britannica.com/art/Latin-American-music) by acquiring the label Exile. The move led to the founding of its [Mexico](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mexico)-based subsidiary **HYBE Latin America**, which plans to begin major operations in 2025.

HYBE 2.0: Redefining global growth
----------------------------------

In August 2024, HYBE began a major restructuring to improve its ability to compete globally. Known as HYBE 2.0, the plan aims to broaden its product offerings, tailor its operations to different regions, and pursue other key initiatives.

Under the leadership of CEO Jason Jaesang Lee, HYBE reorganized its operations into three pillars: labels, solutions, and platforms. The labels pillar focuses on the company’s music production and artist management operations, while the solutions and platforms pillars drive the company’s growth in technology and various supporting operations like IP management and merchandising that complement the company’s music business.

HYBE Music Group APAC was formed to manage all music labels in South Korea and Japan. It is also working to establish operations in multiple countries and explore and produce various music styles (beyond K-pop) in local and international markets.

HYBE America, led by Scooter Braun, was given responsibility for developing a management division focused on signing new artists in partnership with Geffen Records. Meanwhile, HYBE Latin America plans to build production studios in Mexico, with operations set to start in 2025.

HYBE America’s signing of Katseye embodies the company’s vision of hybrid cultural production. Based in Los Angeles, Katseye is a “global” K-pop group with six female singers from diverse countries and cultural backgrounds:

*   Sophia Laforteza, from [Manila](https://www.britannica.com/place/Manila), Philippines 
*   Manon Bannerman, born and raised in [Switzerland](https://www.britannica.com/place/Switzerland), with Swiss-Italian and Ghanaian heritage 
*   Daniela Avanzini, an American from [Atlanta](https://www.britannica.com/place/Atlanta-Georgia) of Venezuelan and Cuban descent 
*   Lara Raj, an Indian-American from Los Angeles 
*   Megan Skiendiel, born in [Honolulu](https://www.britannica.com/place/Honolulu), with Chinese-Singaporean heritage 
*   Yoonchae Jeong, from Seoul, South Korea

On the tech front, HYBE’s Weverse is launching a subscription tier in December 2024 featuring several new fan club benefits such as ad-free video streaming, offline storage for on-demand content, and digital currency. HYBE is also continuing investments in [artificial intelligence](https://www.britannica.com/technology/artificial-intelligence) (AI) and [gaming](https://www.britannica.com/technology/online-gaming).

Challenges and controversies
----------------------------

As HYBE has grown into a global entertainment powerhouse, it has faced its share of disputes and criticisms.

One prominent controversy involving HYBE was its clash with its subsidiary Ador, led by CEO Min Hee-jin, the creative force behind Ador’s flagship girl group NewJeans. The dispute revolved around creative and management control, with Ador accusing HYBE of copying the NewJeans concept. The conflict escalated into a bitter, highly publicized legal battle over HYBE’s alleged overreach and Ador’s autonomy as a sub-label.

South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission launched an investigation into HYBE alleging the company falsified documents and omitted information in its mandatory filings. Despite the probe, HYBE was the first K-pop company listed as a major conglomerate by the antitrust regulator.

In 2024, three HYBE employees faced charges for [insider trading](https://www.britannica.com/money/insider-trading). Prosecutors accused the employees of selling HYBE shares in 2022 shortly before BTS publicly announced its hiatus due to mandatory [military service](https://www.britannica.com/topic/armed-force). The news caused HYBE shares to plunge 25%.

Despite these controversies, HYBE has evolved from a regional music production company into a global entertainment leader. By leveraging its K-pop roots, innovative technology, and cross-cultural approach to entertainment, HYBE has redefined how music is created, distributed, and consumed globally.

Military service in Korea, as in any other country in the world, is demanding and strict.

The life of a Korean soldier in training is hard and difficult.

![Image 5](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-ea4e225d471c48682c68777110b8fac7)

I can only say that we will have to have Yoongi-level patience to put up with so much nonsense that won't be long in coming.

# The Company Behind K-Pop Phenom BTS Is Launching a Blockchain Biz in LA. Fans Are Skeptical.

Kristin Snyder is dot.LA's 2022/23 Editorial Fellow. She previously interned with Tiger Oak Media and led the arts section for UCLA's Daily Bruin.

![The Company Behind K-Pop Phenom BTS Is Launching a Blockchain Biz in LA. Fans Are Skeptical.](https://dot.la/media-library/file-bts-at-the-white-house-on-may-31-2022-04-jpg-wikipedia.jpg?id=31862451&width=2000&height=1500&quality=85&coordinates=0%2C0%2C184%2C0)

Entertainment company HYBE—the corporation behind international phenomenon BTS—partnered with blockchain technology company Dunamu to [launch Levvels Inc](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/levvels-inc-introduces-momentica-the-future-of-fandom-engagement-around-the-globe-through-one-of-a-kind-digital-collectibles-301639575.html). Based out of Los Angeles, the company intends to connect fans with artists through Web3 and NFTs. Its upcoming project is Momentica, an online blockchain platform that will offer collectible assets related to K-pop groups Seventeen, fromis\_9, Tomorrow X Together, Enhypen and Le Sserafim. Its first collection, TAKE, will feature photos, videos, voice recordings and autographs.

HYBE’s latest launch, however, comes at a time when K-pop fans have turned against NFTs. In 2021, the notoriously passionate fanbase [criticized](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2021/12/nft-kpop-environmental-problems/621091/) HYBE’s partnership with Dunamu's last NFT-based business venture over environmental concerns, propelling #ARMYsAgainstNFT to trend on Twitter.

Despite claiming to have a fan-first ethos, HYBE has seemingly ignored fans’ criticisms with the launch of Levvels. Their latest announcement has [fostered](https://twitter.com/monjaymanjay/status/1577131279975186433?s=20&t=kx5odF7VWMDnOi18xEG_4Q) [similar](https://twitter.com/miriagustd/status/1577110988943667201?s=20&t=kx5odF7VWMDnOi18xEG_4Q) [concerns](https://twitter.com/caffekook/status/1577110537384493056?s=20&t=kx5odF7VWMDnOi18xEG_4Q), though not to the same degree. Perhaps because Momentica, Levvels’ first project, uses a cloud-based blockchain service platform that [claims to use 30 million times less electricity](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/levvels-inc-introduces-momentica-the-future-of-fandom-engagement-around-the-globe-through-one-of-a-kind-digital-collectibles-301639575.html) than Ethereum.

Still, the introduction of a new NFT platform joins a [crowded](https://dot.la/michael-le-tiktok-to-web3-2658326027.html?utm_campaign=post-teaser&utm_content=84efnb9u) [Los Angeles](https://dot.la/nft-2651148069.html?utm_campaign=post-teaser&utm_content=19c73ooe) [NFT](https://dot.la/nft-brands-raise-2656965137.html) [space](https://dot.la/tom-brady-religion-of-sports-2657465526.html) even as the crypto markets remain rocky. As such, appealing to a specific fanbase may help give Levvels an edge. But K-pop fans' previous disdain toward NFTs could squash those dreams.

More generally, the continued push for Web3 content reflects K-pop’s general turn towards an increasing number of tech investments: HYBE, considered one of the [big four](https://www.statista.com/topics/5688/k-pop-and-big-4-entertainment-agencies-in-south-korea/) South Korean entertainment agencies, recently [acquired Supertone](https://pulsenews.co.kr/view.php?year=2022&no=850602), an AI company that can clone voices. Last year, Supertone’s tech was [featured on](https://www.thefader.com/2021/02/26/big-hit-entertainment-bts-supertone-clone-voices) the Korean reality show, “Competition of the Century: AI vs Human.” The company used AI to recreate the voice of deceased singer Kim Kwang-seok. In addition to Supertone, HYBE has also [invested](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/hybe-corporation/recent_investments) in a number of international, entertainment-based tech companies.

To that end, South Korean entertainment company CJ ENM recently [invested in Los Angeles-based AmazeVR](https://dot.la/amazevr-raises-17m-concerts-2658355790.html), which will produce virtual concerts for its talent roster. CJ ENM’s other investments include [HYPERREAL](https://www.cjenm.com/en/news/cj-enm-acquires-stake-in-hyperreal-the-metaverse-entertainment-and-digital-human-studio/), a metaverse studio, and [AFUN Interactive](https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com/2021/09/01/business/industry/apoki-cjenm/20210901180200915.html), the 3D graphics company behind virtual musician Apoki.

The metaverse has also been bolstered by K-pop companies. SM Entertainment [formed Aespa](https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/k-pop/news/article/3107417/new-k-pop-girl-group-aespa-red-velvet-managers-sm?module=inline&pgtype=article), a group combining both virtual and physical singers, and its founder [views the metaverse](https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/sm-entertainment-founder-lee-soo-man-talks-the-metaverse-and-his-future-vision-of-k-pop/) as “the future of K-pop.”

Of course, K-pop corporations have long [run their musical acts like businesses](https://asia.nikkei.com/Spotlight/The-Big-Story/Business-of-K-pop-Inside-the-pandemic-proof-empire-of-BTS): [BTS](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/01/30/bts-kpop-bighitentertainment/)—HYBE’s most successful boy band—was formed through auditions, and the group has gone on to make millions through merchandise and sponsorships. But that success comes as K-pop corporations [face pushback](https://jacobin.com/2020/07/bts-k-pop-kpop-black-lives-matter-blm-trump) for heavily controlling their talent to bring in more money. After [going public](https://time.com/5899791/bts-bighit-ipo/) two years ago, HYBE’s interest in tech is more than likely just another way to support its music groups. And NFTs offer an easy method to engage fervent fans through content that would otherwise go unmonetized.

Kristin Snyder is dot.LA's 2022/23 Editorial Fellow. She previously interned with Tiger Oak Media and led the arts section for UCLA's Daily Bruin.

## 🔦 Spotlight

**Happy Friday, Los Angeles!**

This week, LA’s biggest tech and media players made one thing clear: they want to own the relationship. Whether it’s a celebrity sending selfies straight to your home screen or a content giant rewriting the rules of sports broadcasting, the power shift toward more curated, direct experiences is unmistakable, and it’s being engineered right here.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201500%202000'%3E%3C/svg%3E) Image Source : Locket

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201500%202000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**📸 Locket Doubles Down on Star Power**

Venice-based [Locket](https://locket.camera/about), the viral photo sharing app that made homescreen widgets cool, is now leaning into what LA does best: celebrity. Its new feature, [Celebrity Lockets](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/photo-sharing-app-locket-banking-130000795.html), allows artists to send exclusive photos directly to fans’ home screens. Early adopters include Suki Waterhouse and JVKE, with creators curating limited fan access to maintain intimacy and exclusivity. As Locket evolves from a casual social tool into a direct fan engagement platform, it’s becoming an increasingly relevant player in LA’s creator tech ecosystem.

**🏈 Disney’s ESPN Plays Offense**

[Disney](https://thewaltdisneycompany.com/) made a trio of bold moves this week that solidify ESPN’s future and its dominance in sports media. It’s [buying out](https://thewaltdisneycompany.com/espn-nfl-agreement/) the NFL’s stake in ESPN, securing exclusive [NFL Draft](https://thewaltdisneycompany.com/espn-nfl-draft-content-agreement/) and behind the scenes content through 2033, and finally giving its standalone ESPN [streaming service](https://thewaltdisneycompany.com/espns-direct-to-consumer-launch-date/) a launch date: August 21, 2025. That’s a power play straight out of Burbank. At the same time, Disney announced it will no longer report individual subscriber numbers for Disney Plus and Hulu, signaling a shift in how it wants investors and maybe consumers to measure success.

**🗞️ The New York Post Bets on LA**

In a sign of LA’s growing national influence not just in entertainment, but in news, the [New York Post](https://nypost.com/2025/08/04/media/start-the-presses-new-york-post-will-expand-to-la-with-launch-of-the-california-post/) is launching a West Coast vertical called The California Post. With an editorial mission to cover the state’s cultural and political pulse, this move reflects a broader trend of major media brands planting roots in LA to chase both readers and relevance. For local media startups, content creators, and civic tech players, it’s yet another sign that the competition and the opportunity is growing.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201500%202000'%3E%3C/svg%3E) Image Source: Meta

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201500%202000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**📱 Instagram Wants Your Inner Circle**

[Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/) rolled out a [new set of features](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/08/new-instagram-features-help-you-connect/) this week that prioritize connection with close friends. Users can now share what they’re doing, watching, or feeling with a smaller group, clearly borrowing from the intimacy playbooks of apps like BeReal, Snapchat, and yes, Locket. As social platforms shift from mass broadcast to curated circles, LA-based creators and consumer startups should take note: the next frontier might not be going viral, it might be going personal.

From star-powered lockets to streaming shakeups and platform reinventions, this week’s stories highlight how LA’s tech and media companies are rewriting the rules on connection and control.

Snap’s way of saying, "Text me when you get home," but without the follow-up guilt.

## 🔦 Spotlight

**Hello Los Angeles,**

Forget rockets. This week, the loudest move in the defense tech scene came from a factory floor in Torrance, where [Hadrian](https://www.hadrian.co/) secured $260 million to fuel its robot-run revolution.

The company, which builds AI-powered, robot-run factories for America’s aerospace and defense industries, [announced](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/hadrian-raises-260m-to-build-ai-powered-factories-for-america-adds-full-product-manufacturing-opens-arizona-site-302508179.html) the massive Series C raise, led by existing investors like Lux Capital and Founders Fund, along with a factory expansion loan facility arranged by Morgan Stanley. The funding will power Hadrian’s third factory (in Arizona), unlock full product manufacturing, and accelerate its mission to bring American manufacturing roaring back faster, smarter, and more automated than ever.

And here’s what makes them fascinating: Hadrian isn’t just churning out parts. They’re reinventing what a factory **is**. Their facilities look more like giant humming circuit boards than the smokestacks of old, packed with robots, AI, and ambition to move at the speed of software.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20533'%3E%3C/svg%3E) Image Source: Tinder

This West Hollywood based move could redefine trust, safety, and privacy in mainstream consumer apps.

### 🌐 Starlink clears hurdle to launch in India

Elon Musk’s SpaceX backed [Starlink](https://www.starlink.com/) has [cleared most regulatory and licensing hurdles](https://www.ndtv.com/india-news/elon-musk-spacex-clears-regulatory-hurdles-in-india-to-launch-starlink-what-it-means-8806883) with India’s Department of Telecommunications, marking a key step toward launching satellite broadband in one of the world’s fastest growing markets. Final approvals from the national space regulator are pending, and services, expected to deliver high speed connectivity to underserved regions, could launch in the coming months. This is a major milestone for Starlink’s global expansion.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%203840%202160'%3E%3C/svg%3E) Image Source: Apple

The facility, featuring a 4,000 square foot soundstage, spatial audio suites, podcast booths, and more, is designed by Eric Owen Moss and slated to open mid August. It solidifies LA’s reputation as a creative powerhouse and reaffirms Apple’s commitment to investing in and nurturing our city's cultural ecosystem.

From dating apps to deep space to sound stages, LA isn’t just watching the future unfold, we’re building it.

Here’s to independence, imagination, and everything this city dares to launch next. Happy Fourth, Los Angeles.
